newsitem.title: USA: Helms urges halt to U.S. aid to South Africa.
newsitem.headline: Helms urges halt to U.S. aid to South Africa.

text.p: U.S. Senate foreign relations committee chairman Jesse Helms urged U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday to halt U.S. aid to South Africa because of its planned sale of arms to Syria.

He was referring to a $650 million contract for the sale of a South African tank fire control system to Syria and a U.S. law barring assistance to any nation providing lethal military equipment to a country considered by Washington to be a supporter of "terrorism."
"I respectfully urge that you refrain from waiving the provisions of the Anti-terrorism Act," Helms said in a letter to Clinton.

"It is imperative that the administration communicate to the government of South Africa, in no uncertain terms, that no ambiguity exists within the U.S. government about laser-guided tank firing control systems being 'lethal military equipment,' and, consequently, that providing this system to Syria makes it mandatory that foreign aid to South Africa be suspended."
South Africa is due to receive $120 million in U.S. aid in 1996-97.
The U.S. State Department on Monday threatened to cut off assistance if Pretoria went ahead with the deal.

Helms also urged the Clinton administration to cease all activities aimed at settling a dispute involving the South African arms agency ARMSCOR unless Pretoria provided credible assurances the tank equipment would not be provided to Syria.
The United States has imposed an embargo on arms deals with South Africa because of a smuggling case dating from the apartheid era.

"It is unthinkable that the administration would reward the South African arms industry with significant financial benefits resulting from resolution of the ARMSCOR case while the government of South Africa is contemplating a major arms sale to a terrorist nation," Helms said.

Syria had been identified by the U.S. Secretary of State as a state sponsor of terrorism every year since 1979 and "should be treated as a pariah state by all civilised nations until it ceases sponsoring terrorist activities," the Republican Senator from North Carolina said.

There was "substantial American goodwill for the people of South Africa, as evidenced by the provision of $562,400,000 in foreign aid" since the election of President Nelson Mandela in 1994, Helms said.

"It is therefore puzzling that President Mandela and many ANC (African National Congress) members in the South African government are willing to jeopardise South Africa's friendship with the United States for the sake of terrorists who have a history of destabilising the Middle East and targeting American citizens," he added.
